generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, self-regulation is both something you study and a skill you use. The self-regulating learner watches how a strategy is going and amends it when the results fall short, which is the monitoring loop the school's own literature describes. Treating a stalled revision method or a failing analysis approach as information, rather than a reason to work longer, is where creativity enters your own study. A coaching student monitors a session plan, a sport scientist monitors a testing routine, a therapist monitors a rehab protocol; the move is the same, amend rather than merely repeat.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students realise, three weeks into a performance-analysis module, that their usual way of preparing is not working.

Tom notices the method is yielding little but keeps going, reasoning that more hours will fix it. The strategy is never questioned, only intensified. By the assessment, Tom is exhausted and no further forward, having monitored the symptom without amending the cause.

Amara treats the stall as information. The monitoring says the current method is not working, so Amara asks what, specifically, it is failing to do, that is, building no feel for reading match data. She then devises a different approach aimed at that gap, coding short clips by hand before using the software. The new strategy is given a fair trial and reviewed in turn. The problem is solved creatively, from within Amara's own regulation.

Both students saw the same warning sign. Only Amara answered it by amending the strategy rather than merely repeating it.
generatedProse.summary: Self-regulated learning in sport becomes creative at the moment of amendment: when honest monitoring shows a method has stalled and you devise a better route rather than simply trying harder. You can now place strategy-switching in the cycle, appraise when a method is failing, and devise an alternative in your own study. The final lesson turns to creativity in sport scholarship itself.

check.body: A study method you rely on in sport has clearly stopped working. Which response best shows creative self-regulation?

items.text: Work out what the method is failing to do, then devise a different approach aimed at that gap.
Put in more hours on the same method until it pays off.
Switch to a module where the method is not needed.
Keep the method because it has worked in sport before.

feedback.correct: That's right. In sport, you diagnose what the method is failing to do and devise a better route.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that changes the strategy in response to the stall.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Creative self-regulation diagnoses the gap and devises a different approach. More hours, avoidance or loyalty to the old method do not.
